title: One owner, several chances
question: In one round or one pool, does a single owner, sponsor or firm hold more than one chance, under its own name or another?
finding: Housing credits: 11 times one parent company stood behind two or more separately named applicants in the same State round, the most being 4. Community grants: San Francisco Parks Alliance was the fiscal sponsor of 11 of the 19 awards in fiscal 2022, and of 27 awards worth $2.3 million over the four award years on disk. Public Works pools: in 14 cases (10 firms) a firm holds its own contract in a pool and also sits on another member’s team in the same pool. Owner-groups from the aliases analysis tie 2 sets of differently named winners in one round. The 2026 liquor lists, where the State accepts one application per applicant, show no two entrants sharing a registered owner account or business address.
how: Four tests. (1) State tax-credit rounds: applicants are single-project partnerships, and the State prints each general partner’s parent company; applications in one round are grouped by parent. (2) Community Challenge Grants: awards whose grantee line reads "sponsored by" are grouped by sponsor within the award year. (3) Public Works pools: each pool contract number in the status report is looked up in the City’s contract file, which lists joint-venture members and subcontractors; a firm counts when it holds its own contract in the pool and is on another member’s team in the same pool. (4) Every round and pool is checked against the owner-groups; the liquor entrants and storefront-grant recipients are also looked up in the City’s business registry by exact name and compared by business address. The owner-groups built by the aliases analysis were used to count sister companies as one entrant.
limits: None of this is shown to break a rule, and most of it is how the programs are built. In the State’s lists every development applies through its own partnership, so one developer appears under several names; the State prints the parent beside each, so nothing is hidden. A group listed as "sponsored by" another organization applied through that organization; the award pages do not say what the sponsor keeps or controls. Pool contracts carry local-business subcontracting goals (the Port’s reports print the goal beside each contract), an ordinary reason for members to hire one another; whether a firm may be both a member and another member’s subcontractor is set by each solicitation, which is not on disk. The Art Vendor program’s own evaluation says “The current lottery system creates inequitable outcomes as family unit members are permitted to enter the lottery as individuals.”; the licence list carries no household information, so that could not be tested. Registry matching is by exact name and misses businesses registered under another name. Team lists come from the City’s contract file and may be incomplete.
